Vignette: Fatima, Age 63

Fatima grew up in a close-knit Lebanese family where loyalty to one another was understood as something sacred, unspoken but absolute. For most of her adult life, she has channeled that same devotion into precision and order - first as an accountant, then as a senior auditor at a mid-sized financial firm, where she has spent the last two decades reviewing numbers until they tell the truth. She has always trusted that careful attention to detail can reveal what is hidden and prevent what might go wrong. What happened to her son three years ago shattered that belief entirely.

Her son Tariq was thirty-one when he was struck by a vehicle while cycling home from work on a Tuesday evening in October. The driver ran a red light. Fatima received the call at her desk - she remembers the spreadsheet still open on her screen, a column of figures she would never finish reviewing - and drove to the hospital in a state she can only describe now as "not being inside my own body." Tariq survived, but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury. He spent four months in intensive care and has required full-time rehabilitation ever since. He can walk with assistance now, but he is not the man he was. Fatima knows this, and she carries that knowledge like something lodged in her chest.

In the weeks that followed the accident, Fatima barely slept. She would sit in the hospital at all hours, watching monitors, memorizing the rhythm of his breathing. When she did go home, she would lie rigid in the dark and see the accident replaying - not because she witnessed it, but because her mind constructed it from the details she was told, and now she cannot stop seeing it. The car. The intersection. The moment before. She has tried to push the images away, but they arrive without invitation, sometimes in the middle of client meetings, sometimes when she is simply washing a dish.

She returned to work after six weeks because she did not know what else to do with herself. Colleagues noticed she seemed different - quieter, more withdrawn. What they could not see was that sitting at her desk reviewing financial records had become a kind of torment. She finds it nearly impossible to concentrate. She will read the same line of figures four or five times and retain nothing. She, who once caught a rounding error buried in two hundred pages of documentation, now misses things she should not miss. Her supervisor has gently raised concerns. Fatima has said nothing about Tariq to anyone at work.

She has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She tracks every car when she is near a road. She cannot hear a siren without her heart accelerating into something close to panic. She has stopped driving at intersections without traffic lights, taking longer routes to avoid them. She monitors Tariq's caregivers with an intensity that has strained those relationships - she calls multiple times a day, cross-checking schedules, questioning decisions, because she believes that if she had been more attentive before, she might have somehow prevented what happened.

Fatima rarely speaks of any of this. She was raised in a family and a culture where suffering was endured privately, where strength meant continuing. She attends Friday prayers but finds she cannot concentrate on them the way she once did. She feels distant from God in a way that frightens her. She feels distant from herself. She describes her emotional life now as "flat, like a document with all the important information redacted."

She lives alone. She sees Tariq on weekends and helps with his exercises. She watches him struggle to find words he once knew easily, and she smiles for him, and then she drives home and sits in her car in the parking garage for sometimes twenty or thirty minutes before she can make herself go inside.

She does not tell anyone about the parking garage.
